subtitle: Break a big problem into named pieces, and group related data into one unit.

fn.body:
Imagine a restaurant kitchen where every dish is cooked from scratch by one person, every time. Chaos! Real kitchens have stations. A function is a station: a named piece of work you can call whenever you need it.

A function has a return type, a name, parameters and a body: int square(int x) { return x * x; }. Declare a prototype before you use it, so the compiler knows the signature, which is exactly the answer to what a prototype tells the compiler. void functions return nothing. The payoff is threefold: reuse, testing one piece at a time, and readability.
keynotes: A function has a return type, name, parameters and body, as in int square(int x) { return x * x; }.
A prototype declared before use tells the compiler the signature; void functions return nothing.
Benefits: reuse, testing one piece at a time and readability.

scope.body:
Where can a name be seen? That is scope, and a good picture is rooms in a house: what is said inside a room stays in the room. Local variables live inside a function (or block) and vanish when it returns, and each call has its own copy. So two functions can each declare int i without ever bumping into each other.

Global variables are visible everywhere, which sounds handy but makes code harder to reason about, because anybody could have changed them. And static locals are the interesting exception: they keep their value between calls, like a note you leave on the fridge.
keynotes: Local variables live inside a function or block and vanish on return; each call has its own copy.
Global variables are visible everywhere but make code harder to reason about.
static locals keep their value between calls.

stack.body:
What really happens when one function calls another? Picture a stack of plates in a canteen. Each call puts a new plate on top, a stack frame holding the parameters, the locals and the return address. When the function returns, its plate is lifted off and you are back where you were.

Recursion is simply a function calling itself, so many plates pile up. Take fact(4) = 4 × fact(3) = 4 × 3 × fact(2), and so on down, until it reaches the end and unwinds: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. In the figure, five nested frames build up and then unwind, multiplying as they go. Which brings us to a rule you must never forget: every recursive function needs a base case, or the plates pile up forever.
keynotes: Each call pushes a stack frame holding parameters, locals and the return address; return pops it.

rec.body:
Here is a comforting truth: anything recursive can be written with a loop. So why bother with recursion? Because it feels natural for trees and divide-and-conquer problems, where the problem contains a smaller copy of itself. Iteration, in return, is cheaper, because there are no frames to build.

Beware the naive recursion, though. Fibonacci written recursively recomputes the same subproblems again and again: fib(6) makes 25 calls. Step through the figure and see the overlapping calls for yourself. Can you see why a loop that remembers the last two values does the same job with far less work?
keynotes: Anything recursive can be written with a loop.
Recursion is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; iteration is cheaper because it needs no frames.
Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes subproblems: fib(6) makes 25 calls.

struct.body:
A student has a roll number, a name, marks. They belong together, so why keep them in separate variables? A struct bundles fields of different types into one unit: struct Student { int roll; int marks; };.

You reach a field with the dot operator (s.marks), or with an arrow through a pointer (p->marks). Assigning one struct to another copies every field, so t is independent of s afterwards, just as the figure shows.

One subtle thing: size is not always the sum of the parts. A struct { char c; int i; } on a typical machine has c taking 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding so that i is 4-aligned. Total: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 bytes. Padding is the compiler tidying the shelves for faster access.
keynotes: A struct bundles fields of different types, as in struct Student { int roll; int marks; };.
Access fields with the dot operator (s.marks) or the arrow through a pointer (p->marks).
Assigning one struct to another copies every field.
struct { char c; int i; } takes 1 + 3 padding + 4 = 8 bytes.

union.body:
Once you have structs, the combinations are endless. An array of structs models a table, such as a class register of students. A union is the odd one out: all its members share one memory slot, so its size is that of the largest member. Think of one parking space used by whichever vehicle arrives.

enum gives names to integer constants (enum {RED, GREEN, BLUE}; means 0, 1, 2), so your code reads like English. And typedef creates a shorter type name. A union of an int (4 B) and a double (8 B) occupies the larger: 8 bytes.
keynotes: An array of structs models a table such as a register of students.
A union shares one memory slot between its members, so its size is the largest member; an int (4 B) and a double (8 B) occupy 8 bytes.
enum names integer constants (RED, GREEN, BLUE = 0, 1, 2) and typedef creates a shorter type name.
